A trumpet is a musical instrument made of metal — usually a shiny yellow metal called brass. You play it by blowing air through your lips into a small cup-shaped opening at one end, and a loud, bright, powerful sound comes out of a wide, flared opening at the other end. It belongs to a family of instruments called brass instruments (or "the brass section" in an orchestra or band).

Imagine a very long, narrow metal tube. If you stretched it out completely, it would be about 1.5 metres long. But instead of being straight, it is coiled and looped neatly so it fits in your hands. At the end where the sound comes out, the tube flares open wide, like a flower blooming outward. That flared opening is called the bell. On top of the instrument, there are three buttons, called valves, that the player presses in different combinations to produce different musical notes.

The trumpet has a very distinctive sound — it is bright, bold, sharp, and piercing. It can be heard clearly even over a large orchestra or a loud crowd. It can sound triumphant and heroic, joyful, mournful, smooth and jazzy, or energetic and exciting, depending on how it is played.

Trumpets are incredibly versatile and appear in many different types of music:

  • Orchestras and concert bands — In a classical orchestra, trumpets are part of the brass section and are used for powerful, dramatic moments.
  • Jazz music — The trumpet is one of the defining instruments of jazz. Legendary jazz musicians like Louis Armstrong and Miles Davis made the trumpet world-famous in this genre.
  • Military and ceremonial music — Trumpets have been used for centuries in armies and royal courts. The iconic sound of a trumpet call is still used today for ceremonies, salutes, and official events.
  • Marching bands — Trumpets are a staple of marching bands at sports events, parades, and school performances.
  • Pop, funk, soul, and Latin music — Many popular songs feature trumpets to add energy, punch, or colour to the music.
A person who plays the trumpet is called a trumpeter or a trumpet player.

The word "trumpet" as a noun goes beyond the instrument itself:

1. The sound an elephant makes.
When an elephant lets out its loud, high-pitched, powerful cry, that sound is called a trumpet. It is so named because the sound resembles the loud blast of a trumpet instrument.

2. A loud, penetrating sound in general.
In literary or descriptive writing, any loud, clear, resonant sound — like a powerful horn, a blast of wind, or even a voice — can be poetically referred to as a trumpet or described as sounding like one. For example: "The trumpet of the storm woke everyone up."

3. A trumpet-shaped object.
Because of its distinctive shape, some things in nature that are wide and flared at the opening — particularly certain flowers — are called trumpets or described as being trumpet-shaped. For example, the daffodil flower has a long central tube that opens wide at the end, and that central part is often called the trumpet. Similarly, flowers like the trumpet lily and trumpet vine get their names from this shape.
A Common Expression Using This Word

"To blow your own trumpet" is a very common English phrase (especially in British English). It means to praise yourself or boast about your own achievements and abilities — just like a trumpeter loudly announcing their own presence. It is usually used to describe someone who talks too much about how good they are.

Example: "She's always blowing her own trumpet about her promotion."

A trumpet is a brass wind instrument with a coiled tube, three valves, and a flared bell, known for its loud, bright, powerful sound. From this central meaning, the word expands to describe: the loud cry of an elephant, any loud resonant sound, and the flared shape seen in certain natural objects like flowers.
